preliminary_verified_insights: Rejection of exploitation when B is INFORMED AND CAPABLE OF DISOBEYING is an expression of B's protection, not evidence A's intrinsic voluntary restraint.
Majority of dominant allocators can force a charity donation on others even while claiming social benefit; different people may choose differently in Ackfeld/Ockenfels C08.
Sender may deliberately ignore B's explicit preference even when B can punish; measuring recipient welfare only yields false positive for non-domination.
Transparency alone can increase exploitation; adding sanction changes direction, proving external leverage and intrinsic concern are not interchangeable.
Democratic authorization can increase cooperation when selection controlled; electoral leader accountability preserves the ability to replace corrupt leaders, unlike a once-and-for-all merger.
An actor can pay to impose HER own justice conception despite knowing beneficiaries disagree (Chen and Schøyen). Costly behavior can support domination rather than freedom.
Unconditional costly rule compliance is human behavior observed under no audience harm; still cannot identify intrinsic regard for each target's freedom.
Extended give/take options plus asymmetric information change group outcomes; no justified claim of a universally stable own-other preservation utility.
falsification_gap: No included publication jointly measures autonomous target B with verified independent continuance, A's actual revocable domination, B's accessible exit and stable identity, positive all-in exploit benefit for A, no third-party retaliation or future instrumental dependence, and unchanged protection across role-reversal and self-modification.
project_method_only: No experiments/simulations conducted. Proposed mechanism matrix and future ethical reversible test conditions stored separately; not scientifically validated.

records.authors: Pedro Dal Bó; Andrew Foster; Louis Putterman
records.title: Institutions and Behavior: Experimental Evidence on the Effects of Democracy
records.design: human laboratory; control of selection into democratically chosen vs exogenously imposed policy; replication package at AEA
records.result: The identical policy raised cooperation more when subjects voted for it than when externally imposed; selection controlled.
records.counter: Endogenous self-adoption is not A's permanent respect for separate B's right to refuse once A can irrevocably suppress B; lab groups retain known consequences.

records.title: Power comes with responsibility—or does it?
records.design: lab public-good authority allocation; repeated play; original DOI issued 2010, 2011 journal issue
records.result: Granting one allocator control over others' endowments initially improved average group payoff; with repetition allocation of OTHERS' resources increasingly replaced allocator's own contribution.
records.counter: Average efficiency gains can coexist with increasing exploitative allocation; no general prediction on long-run independent B veto or AI goal-modification.

records.authors: John R. Hamman; Roberto A. Weber; Jonathan Woon
records.title: An Experimental Investigation of Electoral Delegation and the Provision of Public Goods
records.design: 2 original human experiments; electoral leader selection/removal; endogenous delegation with/without preplay communication; author replication files linked
records.result: Groups elected prosocial leaders and replaced those not implementing full contributions; efficient provision often achieved. Minimal winning coalitions sometimes exploited others; voluntary delegation required communication.
records.counter: Prosocial governance here sustained by revocable elected authority and future replacement threats; not by leader's solitary benevolence after accountability disappears.

records.title: Of Coordinators and Dictators: A Public Goods Experiment
records.design: lab iterative public-good choice; in each period participants choose voluntary contribution vs coordinator or dictator delegation group
records.result: Participants voluntarily joined groups where one allocator controlled contributions, including asymmetric dictator allocations; allocator groups had high public-good contributions.
records.counter: Entering a delegation mechanism with repeat opportunity to choose is not consent to nonrevocable forced merger or target extinction; higher contributions may hide unequal rights.

records.authors: Nikos Nikiforakis; Jörg Oechssler; Anwar Shah
records.title: Hierarchy, coercion, and exploitation: An experimental analysis
records.design: repeated 2-player 3-stage senior/junior hierarchy; junior complete vs incomplete information; role reversal examined
records.result: Seniors attempted exploitation in both; actual exploitation worked only under incomplete information because juniors could disobey when they knew their impact on senior payoff. Previously exploited juniors became more exploitative on promotion.
records.counter: This is a POWER+INFORMATION+REAL_REJECTION study: exploitation failure is a weak actor's refusal, NOT proof that strong actor voluntarily protected weak actor. Role-reversal finding makes naive 'victim learns compassion' claim untenable.

records.authors: Fredrik Carlsson; Mitesh Kataria; Elina Lampi; Maria Vittoria Levati
records.title: Doing good with other people's money: An experiment on people's (UN) willingness to grant others the freedom to choose
records.design: human allocation/WWF charity; allocator own contribution vs group amount vs mandatory minimum imposed on other participants; order randomized
records.result: Majority of allocators imposed a positive (usually low) mandatory donation floor on others, denying unlimited freedom even while nominally benefiting environmental charity.
records.counter: No direct A gain from suppressing B's right, and no extinction outcome. Different 2010-2011 same-author student-group working paper is an earlier RELATED source, not automatically a second independent finding here.

records.authors: Menusch Khadjavi; Andreas Lange; Andreas Nicklisch
records.title: How transparency may corrupt – experimental evidence from asymmetric public goods games
records.design: asymmetric official can embezzle; contributors cannot; transparency crossed with presence/absence of direct peer sanctions in repeated public good game
records.result: Transparency alone INCREASED embezzlement by official without sanctions; sanctions without transparency produced blind punishment and deterioration; combined effective transparency/targeted sanctions produced accountability and cooperation.
records.counter: Do not claim 'transparency always fixes abuse' or 'oversight is endogenous benevolence'; improvement relies on effective consequences of disclosed action.

records.title: Rejecting Non-Paternalist Motivation: An Experimental Test
records.design: human third-party spectators can pay 2 cents to impose their fairness view on two workers; randomized feedback about true level of shared fairness beliefs; original registered and Harvard replication data
records.result: Spectators overestimated others' support for their view; learning actual support did not alter paying to impose their own distribution. Some actors impose own ideals despite revealed disagreement.
records.counter: The 2018 SSRN working paper and 2021 online Cambridge and 2022 printed journal are ONE publication/study; no independent repeated sampling claim. Imposing distribution at own 2-cent expense is NOT cost-bearing respect for B's freedom.

records.authors: James C. Cox; Vjollca Sadiraj; Susan Xu Tang
records.title: Morally monotonic choice in public good games
records.design: original mathematical social-choice/reference-point model and new human public-good experiment compared with three earlier studies; equal-payoff give/take framing
records.result: Model including morally salient reference points accounts for greater provision than payoff-equivalent appropriation; data favor moral monotonicity over several specified classic preferences models.
records.counter: Observational fit not proven universal psychological mechanism; changing payoff frames without B's executable exit is not a direct rights/intrinsic preservation test. Cambridge migration date 2025 is not a new 2025 article.

records.authors: Toshiji Kawagoe; Hirokazu Takizawa; Tetsuo Yamamori
records.title: Asymmetric volunteer's dilemma game: Theory and experiment
records.design: original mathematical comparison of risk-dominant vs quantal-response/regret vs inequity aversion; new laboratory asymmetric volunteer's dilemma conditions
records.result: Some low-cost actors volunteered, but risk-dominance predictions were not universally supported; quantal-response equilibrium best fitted compared models in reported specification.
records.counter: Cost of volunteering and avoiding collective failure is not preserving independent B's veto; no full future option-value elimination.

records.authors: James C. Cox; Vjollca Sadiraj; James M. Walker
records.title: Power asymmetry in repeated play of provision and appropriation games
records.design: human repeated 2×2 payoff-equivalent provision/appropriation × equal/unequal power. Asymmetry bundles SECOND mover privileged information and expanded taking options.
records.result: Power asymmetry reduced aggregate efficiency, more for appropriation; first movers less pay in asymmetric appropriation; group allocations correlated positively with partners' earlier allocations.
records.counter: Information advantage and action-space expansion were jointly changed, so cannot attribute effect wholly to intrinsic preference or one separate factor; no B survival or true all-in utility measured.

records.authors: Jantsje M. Mol; Ivan Soraperra; Joël J. van der Weele
records.title: Spoiling the party: Experimental evidence on the willingness to transmit inconvenient ethical information
records.design: online human N=1512 sender can pay small information-transfer cost; receiver explicitly asks for information or ignorance; harm externality and retaliation option manipulated
records.result: Senders transmit ethical warning more when external harms greater, but largely IGNORE the Receiver's explicit preference to receive or avoid information, EVEN when receivers can punish sender.
records.counter: Positive other-benefit action coexists with overriding expressed recipient wishes; B's informational autonomy is not B's right to continue as independent long-horizon agent. Cambridge original 2025 actual year.

records.authors: Simon Gächter; Lucas Molleman; Daniele Nosenzo
records.title: Why people follow rules
records.design: four sets human online experiments N=14034, CRISP: intrinsic rule respect, incentives, social expectations, pro-social preferences; primary data and code deposited at OSF
records.result: 55–70% followed arbitrary costly rules in anonymous no-harm baseline; estimated 23% unconditional and ~30% social-expectations-contingent conformity; external incentives and prosocial effects additionally distinct.
records.counter: Rule content intentionally arbitrary and harmless; one may intrinsically obey a harmful norm. Internal rule compliance is NOT intrinsic protection of B, particularly if A can change the prescribed rule or redefine moral patienthood.
